claim: The axial element proteins of budding yeast are flexibly anchored to chromatin by the ring-like cohesin complex.
source: We found that the axial element proteins of budding yeast are flexibly anchored to chromatin by the ring-like cohesin complex.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing cohesin-dependent axis protein localization, physical interaction assays (M-track and co-IP) demonstrating Red1-Rec8 interaction, and transcriptional manipulation experiments showing dynamic repositioning of axis proteins.

claim: The ubiquitous presence of cohesin at sites of convergent transcription provides well-dispersed points for axis attachment and thus chromosome compaction.
source: The ubiquitous presence of cohesin at sites of convergent transcription provides well-dispersed points for axis attachment and thus chromosome compaction.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing Red1 and cohesin enrichment at convergent gene pairs, and genome-wide correlation between cohesin and axis protein binding sites.

claim: Axis protein enrichment at convergent gene sites directly correlates with the propensity for recombination initiation nearby.
source: Axis protein enrichment at these sites directly correlates with the propensity for recombination initiation nearby.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between Red1 peaks and Spo11-linked oligonucleotide counts shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A separate modulating mechanism that requires the conserved axial-element component Hop1 biases axis protein binding towards small chromosomes.
source: A separate modulating mechanism that requires the conserved axial-element component Hop1 biases axis protein binding towards small chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing loss of small chromosome bias in hop1Δ mutants (Figure 5D) and increased Red1 on large chromosomes in hop1Δ.

claim: Axis anchoring by cohesin is adjustable and readily displaced in the direction of transcription by the transcriptional machinery.
source: Importantly, axis anchoring by cohesin is adjustable and readily displaced in the direction of transcription by the transcriptional machinery.
evidence: Supported by copper-inducible promoter experiments showing Red1 redistribution upon altered transcription levels (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The genomic distribution of meiotic DSBs is decidedly non-random.
source: The genomic distribution of meiotic DSBs is decidedly non-random (Gerton et al., 2000; Blitzblau et al., 2007; Buhler et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2011a)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DSB formation and repair occur in the context of a specific chromosome architecture characterized by linear arrays of chromatin loops with the bases attached to a proteinaceous axis, known as the axial element.
source: DSB formation and repair occur in the context of a specific chromosome architecture characterized by linear arrays of chromatin loops with the bases attached to a proteinaceous axis, known as the axial element (Moens and Pearlman, 1988; Zickler and Kleckner, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on meiotic chromosome structure.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae most DSBs occur within the chromatin loops, whereas axis association sites are cold for DSB formation.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae most DSBs occur within the chromatin loops, whereas axis association sites are cold for DSB formation (Blat et al., 2002; Panizza et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations and corroborated by Spo11 oligo data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The axial element in yeast contains the axis proteins Red1 and Hop1, as well as the meiotic cohesin complex.
source: The axial element in yeast contains the axis proteins Red1 and Hop1 (Hollingsworth et al., 1990; Smith and Roeder, 1997), as well as the meiotic cohesin complex (Klein et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational studies.

claim: Red1 and Hop1 physically interact with each other.
source: Red1 and Hop1 physically interact with each other (de los Santos and Hollingsworth, 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Red1 helps recruit Hop1 to chromosomes.
source: Red1 helps recruit Hop1 to chromosomes (Smith and Roeder, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation and corroborated by ChIP-seq data showing loss of Hop1 binding in red1Δ mutants (Figure 5B).

claim: Meiotic cohesin is not essential for chromosomal binding of Red1 and Hop1, but Red1 and Hop1 distribution is highly abnormal in cohesin mutants.
source: Meiotic cohesin is not essential for chromosomal binding of Red1 and Hop1, but Red1 and Hop1 distribution is highly abnormal in cohesin mutants (Klein et al., 1999; Panizza et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations and ChIP-seq data showing altered Red1 distribution in rec8Δ mutants (Figure 4A).

claim: The abnormal axis protein distribution phenotype in cohesin mutants is not due to a loss of sister chromatid cohesion, as axis protein distribution is largely normal on unreplicated chromosomes.
source: Notably, this phenotype is not due to a loss of sister chromatid cohesion, as axis protein distribution is largely normal on unreplicated chromosomes (Blitzblau et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: One of the first functions of Red1 and Hop1 is to correctly localize the essential DSB factors Mer2, Rec114 and Mei4 to axis sites.
source: One of the first functions of Red1 and Hop1 is to correctly localize the essential DSB factors Mer2, Rec114 and Mei4 to axis sites (Panizza et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DSB levels are strongly reduced in hop1Δ or red1Δ mutants.
source: Accordingly, DSB levels are strongly reduced in hop1Δ or red1Δ mutants (Mao-Draayer et al., 1996; Schwacha and Kleckner, 1997; Xu et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reduction in Red1 and Hop1 binding in the absence of cohesin correlates with reduced Spo11 binding and low DSB levels on several larger chromosomes.
source: Moreover, reduction in Red1 and Hop1 binding in the absence of cohesin correlates with reduced Spo11 binding and low DSB levels on several larger chromosomes (Kugou et al., 2009; Panizza et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations and corroborated by ssDNA array data in rec8Δ mutants (Figure 7A,B).

claim: Increased binding of axis proteins on small chromosomes correlates with increased DSB levels and crossover recombination.
source: Conversely, increased binding of axis proteins on small chromosomes correlates with increased DSB levels and crossover recombination (Kaback et al., 1992; Blitzblau et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2011a; Panizza et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations and correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Red1 was reported to favor AT-rich segments on chromosome III at a resolution of 3 kb.
source: Red1 was reported to favor AT-rich segments on chromosome III at a resolution of 3 kb (Blat et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Hop1 has preferential affinity for G-rich sequences and specific DNA topologies in vitro.
source: whereas Hop1 has preferential affinity for G-rich sequences and specific DNA topologies in vitro (Kironmai et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: On meiotic chromosomes, Hop1 and Red1 binding coincides with cohesin binding sites and regular distribution of Hop1 requires cohesin.
source: However, on meiotic chromosomes, Hop1 and Red1 binding coincides with cohesin binding sites and regular distribution of Hop1 requires cohesin (Panizza et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation and high correlation between axis proteins and cohesin shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Cohesin is a major determinant of axis attachment sites.
source: suggesting that cohesin is a major determinant of axis attachment sites.
evidence: Inferred from the coincidence of binding sites and requirement for regular distribution.

claim: The yeast meiotic cohesin complex consists of Smc1, Smc3, Scc3, and the kleisin Rec8, which replaces the mitotic kleisin Scc1/Mcd1.
source: The yeast meiotic cohesin complex consists of Smc1, Smc3, Scc3, and the kleisin Rec8, which replaces the mitotic kleisin Scc1/Mcd1 (Klein et al., 1999; Watanabe and Nurse, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational studies.

claim: Despite the different subunit composition, the cohesin-associated chromosomal sites are highly conserved between mitosis and meiosis.
source: Despite the different subunit composition, the cohesin-associated chromosomal sites are highly conserved between mitosis and meiosis (Blat and Kleckner, 1999; Glynn et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A strong correlation between cohesin sites and regions of convergent transcription has been observed.
source: A strong correlation between cohesin sites and regions of convergent transcription has been observed (Lengronne et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation and corroborated by data in Figure 1B showing enrichment at convergent gene pairs.

claim: Changes in transcriptional activities can result in altered cohesin localization.
source: and changes in transcriptional activities can result in altered cohesin localization (Lengronne et al., 2004; Bausch et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cohesin can encircle DNA from two sister-chromatids.
source: Because cohesin can encircle DNA from two sister-chromatids (Ivanov and Nasmyth, 2005, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cohesin is hypothesized to be pushed along genes ahead of the RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) complex, thus accumulating at convergent regions.
source: it is hypothesized to be pushed along genes ahead of the RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) complex, thus accumulating at convergent regions (Ocampo-Hafalla and Uhlmann, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work proposing this model.

claim: A total of 774 Red1 binding sites were identified by statistical analysis.
source: Statistical analysis (Zhang et al., 2008) derived a total of 774 Red1 binding sites
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data analysis using MACS peak calling.

claim: The identification of 774 Red1 binding sites is in close agreement with previous reports, which identified 656 and 802 axis association sites, respectively.
source: in close agreement with previous reports, which identified 656 and 802 axis association sites, respectively (Panizza et al., 2011; Blitzblau et al., 2012).
evidence: Comparison with cited previous studies.

claim: Red1 binding was particularly strong on the three shortest chromosomes, which displayed a higher overall level of axis protein enrichment.
source: Binding was particularly strong on the three shortest chromosomes, which displayed a higher overall level of axis protein enrichment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) (Panizza et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citation.

claim: Rec8 exhibited no chromosome-size bias, suggesting that this chromosome-specific patterning of axis proteins is not dictated by Rec8.
source: Significantly, Rec8 exhibited no such bias, suggesting that this chromosome-specific patterning of axis proteins is not dictated by Rec8 (see later sections).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The enrichment of Red1 on small chromosomes mirrored a previously noted bias of average meiotic DSB levels, which are also highest on the three shortest chromosomes.
source: The enrichment of Red1 on small chromosomes mirrored a previously noted bias of average meiotic DSB levels, which are also highest on the three shortest chromosomes (Blitzblau et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2011a; Thacker et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations and correlation analysis.

claim: The numbers of axis sites on individual chromosomes were highly correlated with the number of Spo11 cleavage events.
source: Indeed, the numbers of axis sites on individual chromosomes were highly correlated with the number of Spo11 cleavage events (Spo11-linked oligonucleotide counts; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The preferential enrichment of axis proteins on small chromosomes may contribute to the observed chromosome-size bias of meiotic DSB formation.
source: Given that axis proteins are required for the majority of meiotic DSB formation (Mao-Draayer et al., 1996; Schwacha and Kleckner, 1997; Xu et al., 1997; Kugou et al., 2009), their preferential enrichment on small chromosomes may contribute to the observed chromosome-size bias of meiotic DSB formation.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between axis protein enrichment and DSB levels, combined with cited requirement for axis proteins in DSB formation.

claim: DSB hotspots were largely excluded from sites of axis protein binding.
source: Consistent with previous findings, DSB hotspots were largely excluded from sites of axis protein binding (Blat et al., 2002; Pan et al., 2011a; Panizza et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations and Spo11 oligo data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Most axis sites detected by ChIP-seq were broad, ranging from 1 to 3 kb.
source: Most axis sites detected by ChIP-seq were broad, ranging from 1 to 3 kb (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by peak width distribution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Spo11 cleavage activity was strongly depleted in axis sites.
source: Spo11 cleavage activity, as determined by sequencing Spo11-associated DSB ends (Spo11 oligos), was strongly depleted in these sites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by Spo11 oligo mapping data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: DSBs occur preferentially within loop regions that are not bound by axis proteins.
source: This pattern further corroborates the notion that DSBs occur preferentially within loop regions that are not bound by axis proteins.
evidence: Inferred from the depletion of Spo11 oligos at axis sites.

claim: Motif discovery did not yield strong consensus sequences associated with Red1 binding.
source: As is the case with DSB hotspots, motif discovery did not yield strong consensus sequences associated with Red1 binding.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis results.

claim: A repetitive sequence pattern consisting of varying numbers of a 3-bp GAN unit was found modestly enriched at Red1 peaks.
source: A repetitive sequence pattern consisting of varying numbers of a 3-bp GAN unit was found modestly enriched at Red1 peaks (E-value = 6.6e-6), with maximal enrichment at the summits of Red1 peaks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, P-value = 5.0e-4).
evidence: Supported by motif discovery analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The GAN motif was not predictive of Red1 binding and was only present in 16.1% (125/774) of Red1 peaks, indicating that DNA sequence is at best a minor determinant of axis protein binding.
source: However, this motif was not predictive of Red1 binding and was only present in 16.1% (125/774) of Red1 peaks, indicating that DNA sequence is at best a minor determinant of axis protein binding.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis showing low occurrence frequency.

claim: Red1 enrichment was significantly biased toward the ends of ORFs, reaching a summit in the 3′ ends.
source: We found that Red1 enrichment was significantly biased toward the ends of ORFs, reaching a summit in the 3′ ends (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by average Red1 signal analysis across all genes shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 94.6% (732/774) of Red1 peaks were located at the 3′ ends of genes (250 bp on either side of the stop codon).
source: We found that 94.6% (732/774) of Red1 peaks were located at the 3′ ends of genes (250 bp on either side of the stop codon; Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by peak position analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The Red1 bias toward 3′ ends of genes contrasts with DSBs, which are predominantly detected at promoter regions.
source: This bias contrasts with DSBs, which are predominantly detected at promoter regions (Blitzblau et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2011a).
evidence: Comparison with cited DSB mapping studies.

claim: The Red1 signals were strongly enriched within the intergenic regions of convergent gene pairs as compared to tandem gene pairs.
source: Moreover, the Red1 signals were strongly enriched within the intergenic regions of convergent gene pairs as compared to tandem gene pairs (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The Red1 binding signal typically consisted of two peaks at convergent 3′ ends, separated by a region of signal depletion.
source: Closer inspection of convergent gene pairs in two independently generated data sets revealed that the Red1 binding signal typically consisted of two peaks at convergent 3′ ends, separated by a region of signal depletion (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq profiles shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Axis protein binding between convergent genes is subject to positional constraints.
source: These data indicate that axis protein binding between convergent genes is subject to positional constraints.
evidence: Inferred from the consistent two-peak pattern at convergent gene pairs.

claim: Convergent gene orientation is both necessary and sufficient for enrichment of axis proteins at the YKL077W/YKL075C axis association site.
source: These results indicate that convergent gene orientation is both necessary and sufficient for enrichment of axis proteins at this axis association site
evidence: Supported by URA3 insertion experiments shown in Figure 1C demonstrating Red1 binding only at convergent gene pairs.

claim: DNA sequence is not a major determinant of axis protein binding at the YKL077W/YKL075C locus.
source: and demonstrate that DNA sequence is not a major determinant of axis protein binding.
evidence: Supported by URA3 insertion experiments showing Red1 binding depends on gene orientation, not sequence.

claim: 79% of convergent transcript pairs exhibited overlapping 3′ UTRs during the early stages of meiosis.
source: Accordingly, our analysis of published meiotic mRNA-seq data (Brar et al., 2012a) revealed that 79% of convergent transcript pairs exhibited overlapping 3′ UTRs during the early stages of meiosis (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of published mRNA-seq data.

claim: The presence and spacing of the two Red1 peaks appeared directly correlated with the amount of transcript overlap at convergent gene pairs.
source: After ranking the convergent gene pairs according to the extent of overlap of their 3′ UTRs, the presence and spacing of the two Red1 peaks appeared directly correlated with the amount of overlap.
evidence: Supported by ranked heatmap analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Gene pairs with an extensive overlap showed well-separated Red1 peaks, whereas gene pairs with little or no overlap exhibited a single peak at the midpoint of their intergenic regions.
source: Gene pairs with an extensive overlap showed well-separated peaks, whereas gene pairs with little or no overlap exhibited a single peak at the midpoint of their intergenic regions (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by ranked analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Red1 binding was maximally enriched ∼150 bp downstream of the 3′ ends of the respective transcripts.
source: Red1 binding was maximally enriched ∼150 bp downstream of the 3′ ends of the respective transcripts, a behavior also observed for cohesin subunits (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by average enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No overall correlation between nucleosome depletion and the gap between the axis protein binding signals was detected.
source: No overall correlation between nucleosome depletion and the gap between the axis protein binding signals was detected, although there was a decline of nucleosome density at a fraction of the convergent intergenic regions (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by nucleosome occupancy analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Nucleosomes do not position Red1.
source: indicating that nucleosomes do not position Red1.
evidence: Inferred from lack of correlation between nucleosome depletion and Red1 binding gaps.

claim: The local transcriptional landscape shapes axis association patterns.
source: Together, these data imply that the local transcriptional landscape shapes axis association patterns.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between transcript overlap and Red1 peak spacing.

claim: Higher and more confined Red1 occupancy was observed between two highly transcribing convergent genes than between gene pairs with less transcriptional activity.
source: This analysis revealed higher and more confined Red1 occupancy between two highly transcribing convergent genes than between gene pairs with less transcriptional activity (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of high vs. low transcription gene pairs shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ongoing transcription helps to focus axis proteins between convergent gene pairs.
source: indicating that ongoing transcription helps to focus axis proteins between convergent gene pairs.
evidence: Inferred from higher Red1 occupancy at highly transcribed convergent gene pairs.

claim: In gene pairs with differential transcriptional activity, Red1 tends to accumulate downstream of the more highly expressed side.
source: In gene pairs with differential transcriptional activity, Red1 tends to accumulate downstream of the more highly expressed side.
evidence: Supported by ranked analysis of convergent gene pairs by differential expression shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Peaks of equal heights were present in gene pairs with similar transcriptional strengths.
source: Accordingly, peaks of equal heights were present in gene pairs with similar transcriptional strengths.
evidence: Supported by ranked analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Axis proteins are not tightly bound to specific DNA sites but instead are focused between convergent genes driven by some aspect of their transcription.
source: This enrichment pattern suggests that axis proteins are not tightly bound to specific DNA sites but instead are focused between convergent genes driven by some aspect of their transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the reciprocal relationship between transcriptional strength and Red1 enrichment.

claim: Changing the level of gene expression is sufficient to alter Red1 binding patterns at axis association sites.
source: To further test this possibility, we examined whether changing the level of gene expression is sufficient to alter Red1 binding patterns at axis association sites.
evidence: Supported by copper-inducible promoter experiments shown in Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of 5 μM Cu2+ induced a marked shift in the Red1 binding pattern toward the downstream gene at the GCY1/PFY1 locus.
source: Addition of 5 μM Cu2+ induced a marked shift in the Red1 binding pattern toward the downstream gene.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The shift in Red1 binding was further exacerbated upon addition of 20 μM Cu2+.
source: This shift was further exacerbated upon addition of 20 μM Cu2+ (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The transcription levels of convergent genes underlie the dynamic binding patterns of axis proteins.
source: indicating that the transcription levels of convergent genes underlie the dynamic binding patterns of axis proteins.
evidence: Inferred from copper-inducible promoter experiments showing Red1 redistribution with altered transcription.

claim: Refocusing of axis proteins could result from sliding motion or repeated recruitment to a chromatin modification or structure at the 3′ ends of transcription bubbles.
source: Such refocusing could either result from sliding motion or repeated recruitment to a chromatin modification or structure at the 3′ ends of transcription bubbles.
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Cohesin is able to change position in response to transcription.
source: Previous studies have shown that cohesin is able to change position in response to transcription (Glynn et al., 2004; Lengronne et al., 2004; Bausch et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Association with cohesin may explain the transcriptional effects observed for axis proteins.
source: Thus, association with cohesin may explain the transcriptional effects we observe for axis proteins.
evidence: Speculation based on known cohesin behavior.

claim: In the absence of meiotic cohesin Rec8, Hop1 still associates with chromosomes but displays large regions of depletion alternating with dense clusters of binding.
source: Our previous analysis had shown that in the absence of meiotic cohesin Rec8, Hop1 still associates with chromosomes but displays large regions of depletion alternating with dense clusters of binding (Panizza et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation and corroborated by Red1 ChIP-seq in rec8Δ shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Large-scale changes in rec8Δ mutants were associated with markedly narrower Red1 peaks.
source: These large-scale changes in rec8Δ mutants were associated with markedly narrower Red1 peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by peak width distribution analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Red1 was no longer biased to the 3′ ends of genes in rec8Δ mutants.
source: Importantly, Red1 was no longer biased to the 3′ ends of genes (Figure 4B)
evidence: Supported by average Red1 signal analysis along genes in rec8Δ shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Focusing of axis proteins at convergent regions was strongly reduced in rec8Δ mutants.
source: and focusing of axis proteins at convergent regions was strongly reduced (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Transcriptional focusing of axis proteins depends on cohesin.
source: implying that transcriptional focusing of axis proteins depends on cohesin.
evidence: Inferred from loss of focusing in rec8Δ mutants.

claim: The small-chromosome bias of axis protein binding persisted in rec8Δ mutants.
source: By contrast, the small-chromosome bias of axis protein binding persisted in rec8Δ mutants (Figure 4D)
evidence: Supported by chromosome-length analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Red1 is enriched on small chromosomes independently of Rec8.
source: indicating that Red1 is enriched on small chromosomes independently of Rec8.
evidence: Inferred from persistence of small chromosome bias in rec8Δ mutants.

claim: A weak but consistent correlation (Pearson's r = 0.37) exists between axis protein enrichment and the local coding density of the genome in rec8Δ mutants.
source: However, we did note a weak but consistent correlation (Pearson's r = 0.37) between axis protein enrichment and the local coding density of the genome.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between Red1 binding and coding density in rec8Δ.

claim: Regions enriched for long ORFs or tightly clustered short ORFs exhibited increased axis protein association in rec8Δ mutants.
source: Specifically, regions enriched for long ORFs or tightly clustered short ORFs exhibited increased axis protein association (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The effect of coding density on Red1 binding appeared to be cumulative, as longer ORFs displayed higher Red1 binding per kb than shorter ORFs.
source: This effect appeared to be cumulative, as longer ORFs displayed higher Red1 binding per kb than shorter ORFs (Pearson's r = 0.70; Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Red1 signal as a function of gene length shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Enrichment of Red1 on gene bodies was not apparent in wild-type cells.
source: Enrichment of Red1 on gene bodies was not apparent in wild-type cells (Figure 4F)
evidence: Supported by comparison shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Cohesin overrides the cohesin-independent axis recruitment activity.
source: indicating that cohesin overrides this cohesin-independent axis recruitment activity.
evidence: Inferred from the appearance of gene body enrichment only in rec8Δ mutants.

claim: In wild-type cells, Red1 and Hop1 form axis attachment sites by recognizing a feature of cohesin-associated sites.
source: Thus, in wild-type cells, Red1 and Hop1 form axis attachment sites by recognizing a feature of cohesin-associated sites
evidence: Inferred from cohesin-dependent localization patterns.

claim: A cohesin-independent mechanism may contribute additional binding specificity for Red1 and Hop1.
source: but a cohesin-independent mechanism may contribute additional binding specificity.
evidence: Inferred from residual Red1 binding in rec8Δ mutants with preference for coding regions.

claim: The majority of Red1 binding sites were unaltered for their positions in the absence of Hop1.
source: ChIP-seq analysis of N-terminally tagged V5-Red1 revealed that the majority of Red1 binding sites were unaltered for their positions in the absence of Hop1 (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq comparison shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Hop1 is not essential for recruiting Red1 to axis association sites.
source: indicating that Hop1 is not essential for recruiting Red1 to axis association sites.
evidence: Inferred from persistence of Red1 binding at most sites in hop1Δ mutants.

claim: Hop1 seems to modulate the amount of Red1 binding.
source: We note, however, that Red1 binding appeared to increase at some positions (see next section). Thus, Rec8 determines the positions of Red1 along chromosomes, while Hop1 seems to modulate its amount.
evidence: Inferred from changes in Red1 peak heights in hop1Δ mutants.

claim: Red1 DNA association is largely undetectable in hop1Δ rec8Δ double mutants.
source: Strikingly, Red1 DNA association is largely undetectable in hop1Δ rec8Δ double mutants (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Hop1 is required for the cohesin-independent recruitment of Red1.
source: indicating that Hop1 is required for the cohesin-independent recruitment of Red1.
evidence: Inferred from loss of Red1 binding in hop1Δ rec8Δ double mutants.

claim: Hop1 is undetectable on chromatin in absence of its partner Red1 even in the presence of Rec8.
source: Hop1, on the other hand, is undetectable on chromatin in absence of its partner Red1 even in the presence of Rec8 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data in red1Δ mutants shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Red1 and Hop1 associate with DNA as a complex in the absence of cohesin.
source: Together, these data suggest that Red1 and Hop1 associate with DNA as a complex in the absence of cohesin.
evidence: Inferred from mutual dependency in the absence of cohesin.

claim: Hop1 is not required for the recruitment of Red1 to sites of cohesin binding.
source: By contrast, Hop1 is not required for the recruitment of Red1 to sites of cohesin binding.
evidence: Inferred from Red1 binding at cohesin sites in hop1Δ mutants.

claim: With few exceptions, Rec8-HA signals were highly similar in wild-type or red1Δ mutants.
source: Finally, with few exceptions, Rec8-HA signals were highly similar in wild-type or red1Δ mutants (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq comparison shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cohesin recruits Red1 unilaterally.
source: establishing that cohesin recruits Red1 unilaterally.
evidence: Inferred from unchanged Rec8 binding in red1Δ mutants.

claim: The over-representation of Red1 on the 3 smallest chromosomes (2.5-fold over the rest) was nearly abolished, falling to 1.25-fold, in the hop1Δ mutant.
source: In wild-type cells, we observed higher overall levels of Red1 on the 3 smallest chromosomes (2.5-fold over the rest, Figure 5D), correlating well with the higher enrichment of DSB machinery (Panizza et al., 2011) and increased DSB levels (Blitzblau et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2011a) on small chromosomes. The over-representation of Red1 was nearly abolished, falling to 1.25-fold, in the hop1Δ mutant (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by chromosome-length analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Hop1 modulates Red1 deposition in a chromosome-dependent manner.
source: Thus, Hop1 modulates Red1 deposition in a chromosome-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from reduced chromosome-size bias in hop1Δ mutants.

claim: The reduced chromosome-size bias may be due to increased Red1 enrichment on the larger chromosomes in the hop1Δ mutant.
source: Relative scaling of ChIP signals between different experiments by NCIS (Normalization of ChIP-Seq data with untagged control) (Liang and Keles, 2012) suggested that the reduced chromosome-size bias may be due to increased Red1 enrichment on the larger chromosomes in the hop1Δ mutant.
evidence: Inferred from NCIS-normalized ChIP-seq data and validated by qChIP.

claim: qChIP confirmed the direction of Red1 signal change predicted from ChIP-seq at all 12 genomic positions tested.
source: qChIP confirmed the direction of Red1 signal change predicted from ChIP-seq at all 12 genomic positions.
evidence: Supported by qChIP validation shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Hop1 is a chromosome-dependent regulator of Red1 deposition.
source: These results identify Hop1 as a chromosome-dependent regulator of Red1 deposition
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of hop1Δ on Red1 binding across chromosomes.

claim: Hop1 down-regulates accumulation of Red1 on the thirteen largest chromosomes.
source: and suggest that it down-regulates accumulation of Red1 on the thirteen largest chromosomes.
evidence: Inferred from increased Red1 on large chromosomes in hop1Δ mutants.

claim: A doublet of small V5-Red1 peaks was found to flank the yeast centromeres at a stereotypic distance of about 270 bp from their centers.
source: A doublet of small V5-Red1 peaks was found to flank the yeast centromeres at a stereotypic distance of about 270 bp from their centers (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by averaged centromere analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In rec8Δ and rec8Δ hop1Δ double mutants, the centromere proximal peaks of Red1 were strongly decreased or missing.
source: In rec8Δ and rec8Δ hop1Δ double mutants, these peaks were strongly decreased or missing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by averaged centromere analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In hop1Δ mutants, the centromere proximal peaks of Red1 were strongly enhanced.
source: By contrast, in hop1Δ mutants, the centromere proximal peaks of Red1 were strongly enhanced (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by averaged centromere analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Rec8 recruits Red1 next to the centromere against negative regulation by Hop1.

claim: Two Rec8 peaks flanked the centromeres at roughly 345 bp from the center.

claim: Rec8 accumulation aligned with the ends of transcripts surrounding the largely transcript-free zone of the centromeres.

claim: Rec8 binding was unchanged in red1Δ mutants at centromeres.
source: and was unchanged in red1Δ mutants.

claim: Red1 peaks are slightly closer to the centromeres (∼270 bp) than Rec8 peaks (∼345 bp).
source: Red1 peaks are slightly closer to the centromeres (∼270 bp)

claim: Red1 may be sandwiched between the Cse4 hemi-nucleosome and cohesin at centromeres.

claim: Red1-HA-3xH3 depended on Hop1 for its interaction with Rec8.

claim: Only Red1 tagged at the C-terminus depended on Hop1 for chromosomal binding.

claim: Hop1 contributes to the interaction between Red1 and Rec8.
source: Therefore, Hop1 contributes to the interaction between Red1 and Rec8.

claim: Red1 requires its intact C-terminus when interacting with Rec8 in the absence of Hop1.

claim: Rec8 recruits Red1, which further recruits Hop1.

claim: In the presence of cohesin, DSB hotspots were distributed across most of the genome.
source: In the presence of cohesin, DSB hotspots were distributed across most of the genome.

claim: DSB formation in rec8Δ mutants was largely restricted to small chromosomes and the vicinity of Red1 clusters.
source: By contrast, DSB formation in rec8Δ mutants was largely restricted to small chromosomes and the vicinity of Red1 clusters (Figure 7A,B).

claim: DSB formation is limited to the genomic neighborhoods that exhibited persistent Red1 and Hop1 binding in rec8Δ mutants.
source: Thus, DSB formation is limited to the genomic neighborhoods that exhibited persistent Red1 and Hop1 binding in rec8Δ mutants.
evidence: Inferred from spatial correlation between Red1 clusters and DSBs in rec8Δ.

claim: Despite the loss of transcriptional focusing of axis association sites in the absence of cohesin and the overall altered patterns of Red1 distribution, DSB formation within Red1 clusters occurred at the same hotspots as in wild-type cells.
source: Strikingly, despite the loss of transcriptional focusing of axis association sites in the absence of cohesin (Figure 4C) and the overall altered patterns of Red1 distribution, DSB formation within Red1 clusters occurred at the same hotspots as in wild-type cells (Figure 7B).

claim: Hotspot designation does not depend on the precise location of axis binding sites.
source: Thus, hotspot designation does not depend on the precise location of axis binding sites.
evidence: Inferred from unchanged hotspot positions despite altered Red1 distribution in rec8Δ.

claim: The general proximity of axis proteins is sufficient to activate DSB hotspots.
source: These data suggest that the general proximity of axis proteins is sufficient to activate DSB hotspots
evidence: Inferred from DSB formation at wild-type hotspots near Red1 clusters in rec8Δ.

claim: The primary role of Rec8 in controlling DSB formation is to broadly distribute axis proteins across meiotic chromosomes.
source: and that the primary role of Rec8 in controlling DSB formation is to broadly distribute axis proteins across meiotic chromosomes.
evidence: Inferred from restricted DSB formation in rec8Δ correlating with restricted Red1 distribution.

claim: Scc1-containing cohesin was targeted to the same chromosomal sites as Rec8-cohesin.
source: ChIP analysis revealed that Scc1-containing cohesin was targeted to the same chromosomal sites as Rec8-cohesin, indicating that Scc1 can fully substitute for Rec8 in recruiting cohesin to meiotic chromosomes (Pearson's r = 0.93, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Scc1-cohesin did not efficiently recruit Red1.
source: However, Scc1-cohesin did not efficiently recruit Red1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by Red1 ChIP-seq in rec8Δ pREC8-SCC1 shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The DSB distribution of rec8Δ pREC8-SCC1 cells remained similar to rec8Δ mutants and unlike wild-type cells.
source: As a result, the DSB distribution of rec8Δ pREC8-SCC1 cells remained similar to rec8Δ mutants and unlike wild-type cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by ssDNA array data shown in Figure 7C.

source: Consistent with this observation, Scc1 failed to detectably precipitate with V5-Red1 when expressed instead of Rec8 from the REC8-promoter (Figure 6F).

claim: Only meiotic cohesin can efficiently recruit meiotic axis proteins.
source: We conclude that only meiotic cohesin can efficiently recruit meiotic axis proteins.

claim: pREC8-SCC1 did restore transcriptional focusing to axis association sites.
source: Surprisingly, pREC8-SCC1 did restore transcriptional focusing to axis association sites (Figure 7D).

claim: Focusing of axis proteins and axis protein recruitment are separable activities of meiotic cohesin.
source: These data indicate that focusing of axis proteins and axis protein recruitment are separable activities of meiotic cohesin

claim: Rec8, but not Scc1, provides the necessary Red1 contacts for evenly distributing axis proteins, and thus recombination events, along meiotic chromosomes.
source: and suggest that Rec8, but not Scc1, provides the necessary Red1 contacts for evenly distributing axis proteins, and thus recombination events, along meiotic chromosomes.
evidence: Inferred from differential ability of Rec8 vs. Scc1 to recruit Red1 and support DSB distribution.

claim: The dispersed genomic distribution of cohesin rings at convergent genes, and thus ultimately the transcriptional landscape, dictates the preferred attachment sites of the axial element.
source: Our findings indicate that the dispersed genomic distribution of cohesin rings at convergent genes (Glynn et al., 2004; Kugou et al., 2009), and thus ultimately the transcriptional landscape, dictates the preferred attachment sites of the axial element.
evidence: Inferred from enrichment at convergent genes and transcription-dependent positioning.

claim: The enrichment of cohesin between convergent genes is not meiosis-specific.
source: The enrichment of cohesin between convergent genes is not meiosis-specific (Glynn et al., 2004; Lengronne et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: By replacing the Scc1 subunit of cohesin with a meiotic variant (Rec8), cohesin is converted into a landmark for axial element anchoring.
source: but by replacing the Scc1 subunit of cohesin with a meiotic variant (Rec8), cohesin is converted into a landmark for axial element anchoring.
evidence: Inferred from Rec8-specific recruitment of Red1.

claim: Sequence-independent recruitment ensures that the patterning of axis attachment sites readily adapts to changes in gene arrangements.
source: Using oriented URA3 insertions, we demonstrate that such sequence-independent recruitment ensures that the patterning of axis attachment sites readily adapts to changes in gene arrangements.
evidence: Supported by URA3 insertion experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: This mechanism may inherently separate axis attachments from DSB hotspots, which occur in promoters and are inhibited by the immediate neighborhood of axis proteins.
source: Moreover, this mechanism may inherently separate axis attachments from DSB hotspots, which occur in promoters and are inhibited by the immediate neighborhood of axis proteins (Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculation based on spatial separation of axis sites and DSB hotspots.

claim: Mitotic cohesin is enriched on or near transcribed genes in both flies and mammalian cells.

source: and cohesin complexes are required for forming the meiotic loop-axis architecture in mammals (Novak et al., 2008; Llano et al., 2012; Hopkins et al., 2014).

source: Thus, the use of the transcriptional landscape as a dynamic reference for meiotic axis assembly may well be conserved through evolution.
evidence: Speculation based on conservation of cohesin enrichment at transcribed genes.

source: Perhaps, linking both DSB hotspots and axis association sites to landmarks of active, RNAPII-dependent transcription ensures that meiotic recombination remains confined to euchromatic and thus non-repetitive regions of the genome, reducing the potential for non-allelic homologous recombination and genome instability (Sasaki et al., 2010).

claim: Recruitment of axis proteins involves direct physical interaction with cohesin.
source: Our data show that recruitment of axis proteins involves direct physical interaction with cohesin.

claim: Among cohesin subunits, Rec8 plays a pivotal role, as its mitotic paralogue, Scc1, does not interact notably with Red1.
source: Consistent with this observation, Red1 is recruited exclusively to Rec8 binding sites on chromatin by Rec8 in the absence of Hop1. In fact, among cohesin subunits, Rec8 plays a pivotal role, as its mitotic paralogue, Scc1, does not interact notably with Red1.

evidence: Supported by citation to work in S. pombe.

claim: As Scc1-cohesin does not recruit or stably interact with Red1 in S. cerevisiae, Rec8 directly contributes to Red1 binding.
source: Whether this mechanism of interaction also operates in S. cerevisiae is unknown, but as Scc1-cohesin does not recruit or stably interact with Red1 in S. cerevisiae, we suggest that Rec8 directly contributes to Red1 binding.
evidence: Inferred from Rec8-specific recruitment and interaction with Red1.

claim: The meiotic cohesin ring forms a stable protein complex with Red1 and Hop1 to flexibly link the axial element with chromatin.
source: These findings indicate that the meiotic cohesin ring forms a stable protein complex with Red1 and Hop1 to flexibly link the axial element with chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from physical interactions and dynamic positioning data.

claim: Previous data showing that linear elements are lost in the absence of Red1 but remain detectable by electron microscopy (EM) in the absence of Hop1 suggest that Red1, but not Hop1, is required to link axis attachment sites to form linear elements.
source: Previous data showing that linear elements are lost in the absence of Red1 but remain detectable by electron microscopy (EM) in the absence of Hop1 (Rockmill and Roeder, 1990; Klein et al., 1999), suggest that Red1, but not Hop1, is required to link axis attachment sites to form linear elements.
evidence: Inferred from cited EM studies.

claim: Red1 has a well-known ability to oligomerize, which may support the congression of axis sites.
source: Red1 has a well-known ability to oligomerize (Woltering et al., 2000), which may support the congression of axis sites, although other proteins, including Hop1, may contribute to the wild-type structure.
evidence: Speculation based on cited oligomerization property.

claim: Immunofluorescence analyses show Rec8 in continuous tracks, whereas Hop1 and Red1 frequently exhibit more focal staining.
source: Immunofluorescence analyses show Rec8 in continuous tracks, whereas Hop1 and Red1 frequently exhibit more focal staining (e.g., [Smith and Roeder, 1997; Jin et al., 2009] and data not shown)
evidence: Supported by citations and unpublished observations.

claim: EM analysis yields estimates of chromatin loop sizes of approximately 20 kb.

evidence: Supported by citation to EM study.

source: which is only moderately larger than the average spacing of cohesin sites of 10.9 kb (Glynn et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Loops generally do not span more than 2 or 3 potential axis association sites.
source: indicating that loops generally do not span more than 2 or 3 potential axis association sites.

source: We show that Hop1 contributes to Red1 recruitment in three ways. First, Hop1 mediates Red1 binding to a number of chromosomal sites independently of Rec8.

claim: Hop1 contributes to the recruitment of Red1 by Rec8, as revealed by the loss of Red1–Rec8 interaction in hop1∆ mutants when the C-terminus of Red1 is tagged.
source: Second, Hop1 contributes to the recruitment of Red1 by Rec8, as revealed by the loss of Red1–Rec8 interaction in hop1∆ mutants when the C-terminus of Red1 is tagged.
evidence: Supported by M-track and ChIP data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Hop1 is a negative regulator of Red1 accumulation at selected chromosomal regions.
source: Third and most unexpectedly, Hop1 is a negative regulator of Red1 accumulation at selected chromosomal regions.
evidence: Supported by increased Red1 at centromeres and large chromosomes in hop1Δ mutants (Figure 5D,F).

claim: DSB formation is dangerous and thus suppressed in the vicinity of centromeres.
source: It has been noted that DSB formation is dangerous and thus suppressed in the vicinity of centromeres (Pan et al., 2011a)

claim: DSB density is higher on the three smallest chromosomes.
source: and that DSB density is higher on the three smallest chromosomes (Blitzblau et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2011a)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

source: which also enjoy substantially higher meiotic recombination rates (Kaback et al., 1992; Kaback, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

source: These findings predict that preferential DSB formation on small chromosomes should be eliminated in a hop1∆ mutant. This is indeed the case based on Spo11 oligo mapping (P Schlögelhofer, personal communication).
evidence: Supported by personal communication with unpublished data.

claim: The overrepresentation of DSB machinery on small chromosomes is not dependent on Spo11.
source: Earlier results have shown that the overrepresentation of DSB machinery on small chromosomes is not dependent on Spo11 (Panizza et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The preferential accumulation of Red1 is unaffected, if not exacerbated in rec8∆ mutants.
source: Moreover, the preferential accumulation of Red1 is unaffected, if not exacerbated in rec8∆ mutants
evidence: Supported by chromosome-length analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Rec8 binding itself exhibits no chromosome-size bias.
source: consistent with the observation that Rec8 binding itself exhibits no chromosome-size bias.

claim: Hop1 is the key factor mediating compensatory DSB machine accumulation on small chromosomes.
source: These data exclude a role of cohesin in creating this bias and support the conclusion that Hop1 is the key factor mediating compensatory DSB machine accumulation on small chromosomes.

claim: Visibly condensed axial structures may not be prerequisite to efficient DSB formation.
source: Our findings support the view that visibly condensed axial structures may not be prerequisite to efficient DSB formation.

source: In particular, yeast rec8∆ mutants fail to assemble discernable linear chromosome axes by EM (Klein et al., 1999)

source: but remain competent to induce DSBs in chromosomal domains that retain Red1/Hop1 binding.

source: This correlation therefore likely reflects a quasi-local function of axis proteins in hotspot activation that is independent of linear axis formation but this remains to be shown.

source: We previously demonstrated that axis proteins are required for the recruitment of several essential DSB proteins (Panizza et al., 2011).

source: Since axis proteins inhibit DSB formation within ∼800 bp of their binding sites (Ito et al., 2014)

source: the Red1/Hop1-dependent local concentration of DSB factors likely activates hotspots at a distance, involving higher-order chromatin interactions.

source: This model explains why aberrant fine-scale positioning of Red1 in rec8∆ mutants still supported DSB formation at wild-type hotspots.

claim: Axis proteins are not responsible for designating certain sequences as hotspots.
source: The fact that the positions of DSB hotspots remain unchanged in these mutants strongly argues that axis proteins are not responsible for designating certain sequences as hotspots.

claim: Hotspot designation is primarily driven by epigenetic marks associated with gene promoters.
source: This conclusion is consistent with growing evidence (summarized in Borde and de Massy, 2013) that hotspot designation is primarily driven by epigenetic marks associated with gene promoters.

claim: The observed double peaks of axis proteins likely reflect the average distribution of axis proteins within the assayed cell population, rather than the distribution along a single chromatid.
source: Given that the cohesin ring was previously proposed to slide along chromatin in response to transcription (Bausch et al., 2007; Ocampo-Hafalla and Uhlmann, 2011), these data indicate that cohesin sliding controls the sites of axis protein attachment. We note that this system allows DNA to be robustly anchored to the protein axis with enough flexibility to allow dynamic processes such as transcription to proceed undisturbed on the DNA (Figure 8).
evidence: Speculation about population-level averaging.

claim: Cohesin sliding controls the sites of axis protein attachment.
source: Given that the cohesin ring was previously proposed to slide along chromatin in response to transcription (Bausch et al., 2007; Ocampo-Hafalla and Uhlmann, 2011), these data indicate that cohesin sliding controls the sites of axis protein attachment.
evidence: Inferred from transcription-dependent repositioning and cited cohesin sliding model.

claim: The adjustable axis-chromatin interface offered by the cohesin ring may be important during meiotic recombination.
source: In addition, the adjustable axis-chromatin interface offered by the cohesin ring may also be important during meiotic recombination.

source: Although our data indicate that positional flexibility of axis attachment is dispensable for DSB formation

claim: Meiotic chromosome axis components have multiple roles in meiotic recombination, including chromosome pairing, checkpoint signaling and preventing non-productive recombination between sister chromatids.

claim: rec8Δ mutants are severely defective in maintaining homolog-directed repair bias at a hotspot on chromosome III.

evidence: Supported by citation and data from this study showing restored focusing.

claim: The dynamic anchoring of axis proteins may be an important prerequisite for controlled meiotic recombination.
source: Given that targeted DNA repair requires substantial flexibility of DNA ends, these observations raise the possibility that the dynamic anchoring of axis proteins may also be an important prerequisite for controlled meiotic recombination.
